en:
Several years have passed since working from home spread. Many people are happy that commuting time has disappeared and they have more free time. On the other hand, some say the line between work and private life has become unclear, and they actually end up working long hours. Some also feel lonely because they have fewer chances to talk with coworkers.
The change of mood that happened naturally when you went to the office does not happen at home unless you make it happen. What matters is not the place but managing your own way of working. Decide your start and finish times, and close your computer when you are done. Perhaps it is exactly these small habits that are the key to working from home for a long time.

en:
To all staff
From next month, as a rule, meeting materials will not be handed out on paper but shared as data. If you need a printout, please print only what you need yourself. However, for meetings attended by people from outside the company, the person in charge will prepare copies for everyone as before.
Also, because color printing is expensive, it will be limited to materials submitted to customers. Please save the data in the shared folder and tell participants by the day before the meeting. General Affairs Department

en:
When you look around a train, almost everyone is looking at a smartphone. Far fewer people read books than before. It is no wonder people say young people are moving away from reading.
However, it is not that they do not read words. In fact, they meet a huge amount of text every day: news, social media, online novels and so on. Perhaps the problem is not the amount but the way of reading. When you get used to skimming one short text after another, the ability to think about one topic for a long time grows more slowly.
Reading a whole book takes focus and patience. That is exactly why, when you finish, you feel your thinking has become a little deeper. There is no need to give up your smartphone, but I would like to have some time each day, even a little, to read slowly and carefully.

en:
Food that is thrown away even though it can still be eaten is called 'food loss'. In Japan, several million tons of food loss occur each year, and about half of it is said to come from homes.
The main causes of food loss at home are buying too much and cooking too much. People buy more than they need because it is on sale, cannot use it all, and the date passes. Also, quite a few people do not know the difference between the 'best-before date' and the 'use-by date', and throw away food that is still safe to eat. The best-before date is the date until which food tastes good; it does not mean the food cannot be eaten right after it passes.
There are many things each person can do, such as checking the fridge before shopping and cooking only as much as can be eaten.

title_raw: A Small Town and Its People
text:

この{活動|かつどう}で{興味深|きょうみぶか}いのは、{助|たす}けられる{側|がわ}だけでなく、{助|たす}ける{側|がわ}も{元気|げんき}になっていることだ。{退職|たいしょく}して{家|いえ}にいることが{多|おお}かった{男性|だんせい}が、{活動|かつどう}を{通|とお}して{地域|ちいき}に{知|し}り{合|あ}いが{増|ふ}え、{生|い}きがいを{感|かん}じるようになったという{話|はなし}も{聞|き}いた。

en:
In the town where I live, nearly 40 percent of the population are elderly people aged 65 or over. Many young people leave for the cities when they go to university or start work, and never come back. The shops on the shopping street are closing one after another.
In this situation, a few years ago residents started a 'watching-over activity'. Neighbors regularly visit the homes of elderly people who live alone and ask if they have any problems. Now many elderly people are said to look forward to the visits.
What is interesting about this activity is that not only the people being helped but also the helpers have become more lively. I also heard about a man who stayed home a lot after retiring; through the activity he made more friends in the area and started to feel his life had purpose.
We may not be able to stop the population from falling. But if there are connections between people, perhaps a town can stay rich even as it gets smaller.

City Library: Guide to Using the Library
- Opening hours: weekdays 9:00-20:00; weekends and holidays 9:00-17:00 (closed every Monday; if Monday is a holiday, closed the next day)
- Borrowing: up to 10 books per person for 2 weeks. Up to 2 DVDs for 1 week.
- Extensions: if no one else has reserved it, you can extend once by 2 weeks. DVDs cannot be extended.
- Returns: on closed days or after closing, use the return box next to the entrance. However, to prevent damage, always return DVDs at the counter.
- To make a library card, you need something that shows your address (such as a driver's license).

en:
A
Uniforms have many good points. Students do not have to worry every morning about what to wear, and differences in families' financial situations become harder to see. Also, wearing the same clothes creates a sense of being a member of the school. It is true that they are expensive, but considering they are worn for three years, they are by no means a waste.
B
Are uniforms really necessary? A full set costs tens of thousands of yen, which is no small burden on a household. It is also inconvenient that you cannot choose clothes to match the heat or cold. Recently, more schools let students choose trousers or a skirt regardless of gender. Instead of deciding everything the same way for everyone, there should be a system where students can choose.

en:

Recently, more people eat out alone, and more restaurants have seats for one person. It is relaxing to eat what you like at your own pace without having to worry about anyone. Enjoying time alone is by no means a lonely thing.
B
I understand that eating alone is easy. But meals should also originally be an important time that connects people. Sitting around the same table with family or friends and talking about what happened that day: shouldn't we think more seriously about the fact that such time is decreasing?

text:
{子|こ}どものころ、{私|わたし}は{失敗|しっぱい}するのが{何|なに}より{怖|こわ}かった。テストで{悪|わる}い{点|てん}を{取|と}ること、{人前|ひとまえ}で{間違|まちが}えること、{友達|ともだち}に{笑|わら}われること。だから、できそうなことしかやらなかった。
その{考|かんが}えが{変|か}わったのは、{社会人|しゃかいじん}になって{三年目|さんねんめ}のことだ。{初|はじ}めて{任|まか}された{企画|きかく}が、{準備|じゅんび}{不足|ぶそく}で{大失敗|だいしっぱい}に{終|お}わった。{落|お}ち{込|こ}む{私|わたし}に、{上司|じょうし}は「{失敗|しっぱい}したのは、{挑戦|ちょうせん}したからだ。{何|なに}もしなければ{失敗|しっぱい}もしない。{大事|だいじ}なのは、そこから{何|なに}を{学|まな}ぶかだ」と{言|い}った。
その{後|ご}、{私|わたし}は{失敗|しっぱい}の{原因|げんいん}を{一|ひと}つ{一|ひと}つ{書|か}き{出|だ}し、{次|つぎ}の{企画|きかく}に{生|い}かした。{結果|けっか}、{二度目|にどめ}の{企画|きかく}は{成功|せいこう}した。{失敗|しっぱい}がなければ、この{成功|せいこう}もなかっただろう。
{今|いま}でも{失敗|しっぱい}は{怖|こわ}い。しかし、{失敗|しっぱい}を{避|さ}けることばかり{考|かんが}えていては、{成長|せいちょう}の{機会|きかい}を{自分|じぶん}で{捨|す}ててしまうことになる。そう{気|き}づいてから、{私|わたし}は{少|すこ}しだけ{勇気|ゆうき}を{出|だ}せるようになった。
en:
As a child, I was afraid of failing more than anything. Getting bad test scores, making mistakes in front of people, being laughed at by friends. So I only did things I thought I could do.
That way of thinking changed in my third year as a working adult. The first project I was put in charge of ended in a big failure because of poor preparation. When I was feeling down, my boss said, 'You failed because you tried. If you do nothing, you don't fail either. What matters is what you learn from it.'
After that, I wrote down the causes of the failure one by one and used them in my next project. As a result, the second project succeeded. Without the failure, this success would not have happened.
I am still afraid of failing. But if you think only about avoiding failure, you end up throwing away chances to grow. Since I realized that, I have become able to be a little braver.
